criterion_notes.c1: Examines a municipal drinking-water conveyance pipeline project (Adduction d'eau potable Grombaou) supplying piped water to drought-affected rural Kanak villages (tribes of Noeli, Tiaoue, and Poindah) and planned branch connections for three unserved houses in lower Neami in the commune of Kone.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording = yes; narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading = no. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study examines institutional and political governance dynamics—specifically a conflict of authority and legitimacy between elected municipal officials (Municipality Council of Kone) and tribal customary representatives (Council of Elders of Neami) against the backdrop of post-Noumea Agreement decolonization and unsettled boundaries between statutory municipal governance and customary authority. Under the mandatory 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, however, Criterion 2 is not met: the paper does not examine a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements for connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules governing consumers, regulatory/administrative discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Instead, it examines political contestation, consultation grievances, rejected demands for upstream resource-extraction royalties, and multi-year public-works capital project delivery (trunk pipe routing and Development Contract budgeting) as an ethnographic window into ideological cleavages within Kanak politics.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative ethnographic evidence from fieldwork conducted in Kone between 2002 and 2004, including participant observation of internal Municipality Council meetings (7 June 2004), interviews with councillors, textual analysis of the 7 June 2004 protest letter from the Council of Elders of Neami, and direct observation of the 19 July 2004 negotiation meeting in Neami.
criterion_notes.c4: Descriptively reports community and household water-service availability and project-completion outcomes: dry-season water shortages in Noeli, Tiaoue, and Poindah; three houses in lower Neami lacking piped water pending the 2005-2009 Development Contract; and completion/inauguration of the Grombaou pipeline delivering water to Poindah, Tiaoue, and Noeli once the elders withdrew their obstruction threat (although the author's primary analytical focus is political legitimacy).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (Municipality Council and Kanak villages/tribes in Kone, New Caledonia), the political/project-delivery exposure, descriptive water-supply and political negotiation outcomes, and an ethnographic case-study design, though the exposure falls outside Criterion 2's rule-type mechanism scope.

study_design: Ethnographic case study (participant observation and documentary analysis)
population_and_sample: Municipality Council (Mairie) officials and rural Kanak tribal communities/Councils of Elders (Neami, Noeli, Tiaoue, and Poindah; approx. 20 Neami inhabitants and 10 municipal staff observed at the 19 July 2004 negotiation) in the commune of Kone, Northern Province, New Caledonia
exposure: Political and institutional rivalry between FLNKS elected municipal officials and tribal customary elders (within post-Noumea Agreement decolonization politics) over public-works pipeline routing, consultation, multi-year Development Contract capital staging, and rejected raw-water royalty demands in the AEP Grombaou water conveyance project
outcome: Withdrawal of the Neami Council of Elders' threat to obstruct pipeline construction and inauguration of piped drinking-water delivery from Grombaou to Poindah, Tiaoue, and Noeli, while connection of three unserved houses in lower Neami awaited the 2005-2009 Development Contract
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this ethnographic study examines a municipal drinking-water conveyance project serving rural Kanak villages (c1 = yes, c3 = yes) and notes pipeline inauguration and unserved houses (c4 = yes), it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification. Rather than analyzing a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure requirements for connection, consumer tariff rules, administrative discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure), the paper uses a dispute over public-works project delivery—pipeline routing, multi-year capital budgeting, consultation grievances, and rejected demands for upstream resource royalties—to examine ideological cleavages between pro-independence FLNKS politicians and emerging customary/indigenous activism in New Caledonia.
